gloss: cut in, engrave; fix, prescribe; what is fixed, statute
summary: חָקַק is to cut into a surface: to hew a tomb in rock, engrave a city on a brick, inscribe words on a scroll, and so to fix something in writing, to decree; its participle מְחֹקֵק is the one who decrees, the commander or lawgiver, and his staff (Gen 49:10; Isa 33:22). חֹק and חֻקָּה are what has been fixed: a portion allotted, the priests’ due, a limit set for the sea, and above all the statutes Yahweh gave Israel to walk in, among them the feasts of Lev 23, each “a statute for ever throughout your generations” (Lev 23:14). Arabic ḥaqq, with the same ḥ, is what is due, binding and true, and Aramaic has the verb “hollow out, engrave”.

words.gloss: what is fixed: an allotted portion, a due, a limit; a decree, statute

senses.definition: A fixed share given to someone, of food or land: what is set aside as theirs.

evidence.note: The priests had a חֹק from Pharaoh and ate their חֹק, so they did not sell their land.
“Feed me with the bread of my חֹק”, set against poverty and riches.
She gives food to her house and a חֹק to her young women.
Yahweh diminished Jerusalem’s חֹק.
Job treasured the words of God’s mouth more than his own חֹק.

senses.definition: The part of the offerings fixed as the priests’ and their sons’, given them from Israel’s sacrifices.

evidence.note: “It is your חֹק and your sons’ חֹק from the offerings of Yahweh made by fire.”
The breast and thigh are Aaron’s and his sons’ “for a חֹק עוֹלָם from the sons of Israel”.
The holy offerings given as a חֹק עוֹלָם, a covenant of salt.

senses.definition: A fixed amount of work required of someone.

evidence.note: Israel’s officers are beaten: “Why have you not completed your חֹק in making brick?”

senses.definition: A line set that something may not pass: the bound Yahweh sets for the sea, the waters and a man’s days.

evidence.note: Yahweh placed the sand as a boundary for the sea, a חֹק עוֹלָם it cannot pass.
When he set for the sea its חֹק, that the waters should not pass his command.
“I broke for it my חֹק and set bars and doors.”
He has marked out a חֹק on the face of the waters, to the bound of light and darkness.
Man’s days are determined; “you have set his חֹק and he cannot pass it.”
Sheol opens its mouth “without חֹק”, without limit.

senses.definition: A single thing fixed by one with authority: Yahweh’s decree over the rain, the heavens, and his king, his statute to Israel, and a king’s or people’s fixed ordinance.

evidence.note: At Marah he set for them a חֹק and a judgment, and there he tested them.
“I will recount the חֹק: Yahweh said to me, You are my son.”
The blowing of the shofar at the new moon is “a חֹק for Israel, a judgment of the God of Jacob”.
The covenant with Abraham confirmed to Jacob for a חֹק.
The heavens and waters: “he has given a חֹק, and it will not pass away.”
When he made a חֹק for the rain.
Joseph made the fifth part to Pharaoh a חֹק in Egypt to this day.
David makes the equal share for those who stayed by the baggage a חֹק and a judgment for Israel.
It became a חֹק in Israel that the daughters lamented Jephthah’s daughter.

senses.definition: In the plural, the things Yahweh fixed for Israel to keep and do, named with his judgments and commandments; to walk in them is life in the land, to cast them off is to leave him.

evidence.note: “Hear the חֻקִּים and the judgments which I teach you to do, that you may live.”
Keeping them is Israel’s wisdom before the peoples, who will hear all these חֻקִּים.
Yahweh commanded these חֻקִּים for Israel’s good always, to keep them alive.
The king reads the law all his days to keep these חֻקִּים.
“Teach me your חֻקִּים.”
“Your חֻקִּים have been my songs in the house of my sojourning.”
He declares his חֻקִּים and judgments to Israel; he has not dealt so with any nation.
“From the days of your fathers you have turned aside from my חֻקִּים.”
“Remember the law of Moses my servant, the חֻקִּים and judgments.”
Ezra set his heart to seek the law of Yahweh, to do it, and to teach חֹק and judgment in Israel.
Of the rebellious generation: “I gave them חֻקִּים that were not good.”

senses.definition: Once, in the plural with “heart”: what a man fixes in his mind, his resolve.

evidence.note: By the divisions of Reuben were great חִקְקֵי־לֵב, resolves of heart (beside “searchings of heart” in Jdg 5:16).

evidence.locator: חֹק → δικαίωμα ×16 (lemma count, MACULA alignment); Gen.26.5, חֻקּוֹתַי → δικαιώματά

evidence.note: Zacharias and Elisabeth walk in all the commandments and δικαιώματα of the Lord.
The first covenant had δικαιώματα of service.

parallels.note: The fixed pair “statutes and judgments”: what is fixed beside what is judged right.
Beside the law and the commandments, as the things Yahweh gives Israel to keep.

phrases.gloss: a perpetual due; a lasting bound
the bread of my portion, my allotted bread

words.gloss: what is fixed: a statute, ordinance; a fixed order or custom

senses.gloss: statute of a rite or feast
senses.definition: The fixed ordinance by which a feast, offering or rite is to be kept, often “a statute for ever throughout your generations”.

evidence.note: No bread or parched grain until the day of the firstfruits: “a חֻקַּת עוֹלָם throughout your generations in all your dwellings.”
The day of the feast of weeks, a holy convocation.
The Day of Atonement: no work.
The seven days of booths in the seventh month.
The Passover day is a memorial, kept as a feast “a חֻקַּת עוֹלָם”.
“According to all the חֻקָּה of the Passover they shall keep it.”
One חֻקָּה for the sojourner and the native.
The tenth day of the seventh month.
The lamps kept burning before Yahweh from evening to morning.
“The priesthood shall be theirs for a חֻקַּת עוֹלָם.”
The red heifer, “the חֻקָּה of the law”.
The daughters of Zelophehad’s case becomes a חֻקַּת מִשְׁפָּט, a statute of judgment.
“These are the חֻקּוֹת of the altar” in the house Ezekiel is shown.

senses.definition: The ordinances Yahweh gives as a way of life: his people walk in them and keep them, and the man who does them lives by them.

evidence.note: “Keep my חֻקֹּת and my judgments, which if a man does, he shall live by them.” Quoted at Rom 10:5 and Gal 3:12.
Yahweh gave Israel his חֻקּוֹת in the wilderness, by which a man lives.
Abraham kept Yahweh’s charge, commandments, חֻקּוֹת and laws.
With a new heart and spirit “they will walk in my חֻקּוֹת”.
Under David his servant, one shepherd, they will walk in his judgments and keep his חֻקּוֹת.
Solomon walked in the חֻקּוֹת of David his father.
Moses writes of the righteousness of the law that the man who does them shall live by them (Lev 18:5).

senses.definition: The fixed practices of other peoples, or of a king who leads into them, which Israel is not to walk in.

evidence.note: Not to do as Egypt and Canaan do, nor walk in their חֻקּוֹת.
Israel walked in the חֻקּוֹת of the nations Yahweh drove out.
“The חֻקּוֹת of the peoples are vanity”: a tree cut from the forest and worked into an idol.
“The חֻקּוֹת of Omri are kept.”

senses.definition: The fixed courses Yahweh set for sun, moon, stars, sea and seasons.

evidence.note: Yahweh gives the sun for light by day, the חֻקֹּת of the moon and stars for light by night.
“If I have not set the חֻקּוֹת of heaven and earth.”
“Do you know the חֻקּוֹת of the heavens?”
Yahweh keeps for us “the weeks, the חֻקּוֹת of harvest”, the fixed weeks of harvest.

evidence.locator: חֻקָּה → δικαίωμα ×16 (lemma count); Gen.26.5, חֻקּוֹתַי → δικαιώματά; Lev.23.14 and Lev.23.41 render חֻקַּת עוֹלָם by νόμιμον αἰώνιον, a word the New Testament does not use

evidence.note: That the δικαίωμα of the law might be fulfilled in us who walk according to the Spirit (compare Ezk 36:27).
Ordinances of the flesh, imposed until a time of setting right.

parallels.note: “My statutes and my judgments”, kept and done together.
Beside his commandments, as what Israel is to keep.

phrases.gloss: a statute for ever throughout your generations

stems.gloss: cut in, engrave, inscribe; mark out; decree

senses.definition: Cut lines or a hollow into a hard surface: hew a tomb in the rock, engrave a city on a brick or figures on a wall, inscribe words to last.

evidence.note: Shebna hews out a grave on high and “cuts in the rock” a dwelling for himself.
Take a brick and engrave on it a city, Jerusalem.
Images of the Chaldeans engraved in vermilion on the wall.
Write it on a tablet and inscribe it in a scroll, as a witness for the time to come.
“Behold, I have engraved you on my palms.”

senses.definition: Draw a fixed line or outline, of Yahweh marking out the circle of the deep and the foundations of the earth.

evidence.note: When he inscribed a circle on the face of the deep.
When he marked out the foundations of the earth.

senses.definition: Fix in writing as binding, decree; the participle is one who decrees, a commander.

evidence.note: Woe to those who decree decrees of iniquity, and the writers who write oppression: decreeing set beside writing.
My heart is toward the commanders of Israel.

stems.gloss: decree; (participle מְחֹקֵק) lawgiver, commander; ruler’s staff

senses.definition: Fix what is to be done, of rulers decreeing right.

evidence.note: By wisdom kings reign and rulers decree righteousness.

senses.definition: The one who decrees: a commander of a tribe, and Yahweh as Israel’s lawgiver beside judge and king.

evidence.note: “Yahweh is our judge, Yahweh is our מְחֹקֵק, Yahweh is our king; he will save us.”
From Machir came down מְחֹקְקִים.
Gad: there the portion of a מְחֹקֵק was reserved.

senses.definition: The staff that marks the one who commands, set beside the sceptre.

evidence.note: “The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a מְחֹקֵק from between his feet, until Shiloh comes.” “Between his feet” fits a staff; the parallel fits the ruler who holds it.
The nobles dug the well “with the מְחֹקֵק, with their staffs”.
“Judah is my מְחֹקֵק”, beside Ephraim the helmet of my head.

senses.definition: The participle: what has been fixed as law.

evidence.note: Lest the king drink and forget what is decreed and pervert the judgment of the afflicted.

senses.definition: Be cut into a lasting record.

evidence.note: “Oh that my words were written, that they were inscribed in a book!”, then cut in rock for ever (Job 19:24).

words.summary: A by-form of חָקַק with a weak third letter, used only of carving and tracing, in the same sense as חָקַק “cut in”. Kept here as a word of this root; its own root key is חקה.

senses.definition: Cut in relief or outline on a surface: the cherubim and palms of the temple, and images on a wall.

evidence.note: Gold fitted over the carved work.
Every form of creeping thing and beast and idol carved on the wall.
Men carved on the wall, beside חָקַק “engraved” in the same verse.

senses.definition: Mark a line about something, so that it cannot go past it.

evidence.note: “You put my feet in the stocks … you trace a line round the soles of my feet.”

cognates.gloss: be established, binding, due, true; a right, a due, truth
cognates.note: Lane’s sources give the verb as “it was, or became, established, confirmed … necessary, binding, obligatory, incumbent, or due”, and the noun as what is right, true and binding, and one’s right or due (pl. ḥuqūq); form X istaḥaqqa “demand as one’s right, be entitled to”. This answers to חֹק as an allotted portion and a due (Gen 47:22; Lev 10:13) and to what is fixed as binding. Arabic ḥ (ح), not ḫ (خ), stands behind ח.

cognates.gloss: a receptacle cut or shaped out; a small hollow, a socket
cognates.note: A receptacle “of wood, or of ivory, or of some other material proper to be cut, or shaped out”, and the hollow or socket of a joint. If it belongs to the same Arabic root, it shows the physical “cut, hollow out” of Hebrew חָקַק and Aramaic חֲקַק with the same ḥ as ḥaqq “due, binding”: one older root covering both the cutting and what is fixed. Recorded as possible because Lane gives no link between these and ḥaqq.

cognates.gloss: hollow out; (passive participle) engraved, marked; (ithpaal) be engraved
cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic, of hollowing out a reed and of engraved stones (Targ. Y. Exo 28:11) and marked skin (Targ. Y. Lev 19:28, for Hebrew קַעֲקַע). Aramaic ח does not show whether ḥ or ḫ stands behind it.

evidence.note: Lev. R. s. 6; Targ. Y. Ex. 28:11; Targ. Y. Lev. 19:28; Ithpa. Targ. Y. Ex. 20:2–3.

doctrine.statement: Each of the feasts of Lev 23 is fixed as “a חֻקַּת עוֹלָם throughout your generations in all your dwellings” (Lev 23:14, 21, 31, 41), as are the Passover (Exo 12:14), the Day of Atonement (Lev 16:29–34) and Aaron’s priesthood (Exo 29:9). Hebrews says that the first covenant had δικαιώματα of service and an earthly holy place, ordinances of the flesh “imposed until a time of setting right”, and that Christ came as high priest of the good things to come and entered once for all by his own blood (Heb 9:1, 10–12); that the priesthood being changed, there is of necessity a change of the law (Heb 7:12); and Paul calls feast, new moon and sabbath a shadow of things to come, whose body is Christ’s (Col 2:16–17). Ezekiel, shown a house still to be built, is given “the חֻקּוֹת of the altar” and priests who keep Yahweh’s statutes in all his appointed feasts (Ezk 43:18; 44:24). From the verses: the statutes were fixed to last as long as the order they belonged to, and the New Testament places that order as a shadow whose substance is Christ.

Yahweh gave Israel his חֻקּוֹת and judgments, “which if a man does, he shall live by them” (Lev 18:5), and Israel in the wilderness did not walk in them (Ezk 20:11–13, 21). Paul quotes Lev 18:5 as the righteousness of the law, set against the righteousness of faith (Rom 10:5–6; Gal 3:11–12). Yahweh promises a new heart and his spirit within, “and I will cause you to walk in my חֻקִּים” (Ezk 36:26–27; 11:19–20), under David his servant as one shepherd (Ezk 37:24). Paul writes that God sent his own Son, so that the δικαίωμα of the law might be fulfilled in those who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit (Rom 8:3–4). From the verses: the statutes describe the life God requires, which the people could not keep of themselves; he undertakes to put his spirit in them so that they walk in his statutes, and Paul finds this done through his Son.

Jacob says that neither sceptre nor מְחֹקֵק will depart from Judah until Shiloh comes, and to him will be the obedience of the peoples (Gen 49:10). Isaiah names Yahweh himself Israel’s מְחֹקֵק, with judge and king, “he will save us” (Isa 33:22). James writes, “There is one lawgiver and judge, who is able to save and to destroy” (Jas 4:12), and Hebrews notes that our Lord sprang from Judah (Heb 7:14), whom John sees as the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Rev 5:5). From the verses: the right to decree belongs to Yahweh, the one who saves, and it is held in Judah by the one to whom the peoples come; so one who judges a brother sets himself where only the lawgiver stands (Jas 4:11–12).

When Zion says, “Yahweh has forsaken me”, Yahweh answers that a woman may forget her nursing child, “yet I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on my palms; your walls are continually before me” (Isa 49:14–16). The verb is the one used of cutting into stone and inscribing what is to last (Isa 22:16; 30:8; Job 19:23–24). From the verses: Yahweh’s remembrance of his people is likened not to a thing written that may be erased but to a mark cut into his own hands.

Yahweh, who gives the sun for light by day and the חֻקֹּת of the moon and stars by night, says that only if those חֻקִּים depart from before him will the seed of Israel cease from being a nation before him (Jer 31:35–36); and if he has not set the חֻקּוֹת of heaven and earth, then he will cast away the seed of Jacob and David (Jer 33:25–26). He set the sea its חֹק that the waters should not pass his command (Pro 8:29; Jer 5:22). From the verses: the fixed order of creation is the pledge Yahweh himself gives for his faithfulness to his covenant people; his promises are as fixed as the bounds he set the sea.

note: Drafted 2026-11-11. Left out: the place names חֻקֹק / חוּקֹק Hukok (h.ff.ad, h.ff.ae; Jos 19:34, 1Ch 6:60), which belong in names/; h.fd.ae and h.fe.ab are cross-references with no tokens; h.ff.af (חִקְקֵי, Jdg 5:15) is counted under חֹק (h.ff.ab), where its sense “resolve of heart” is kept. Included as a by-form: חָקָה (h.fe.aa, root key חקה), pual “carved” and hithpael “trace a line”, sharing חָקַק’s sense; the name חֲקוּפָא (h.fe.ac) is left out. The brief tags Psa 60:9 and 108:9 מְחֹקְקִי as piel; they are entered under the poel participle with the other מְחֹקֵק forms. Pro 8:29 בְּחוּקוֹ is entered under the qal (“mark out”) and its earlier clause שׂוּמוֹ לַיָּם חֻקּוֹ under the noun. Open questions: (1) Gen 49:10 מְחֹקֵק is kept under “staff” because of “from between his feet”; it could as well be the commander himself, and the doctrine uses it either way. (2) Whether the physical “cut” sense and the “due, binding” sense are one older root: Arabic shows ḥ for ḥaqq “due”, and, if ḥuqqa belongs with it, ḥ for “hollow out” too (recorded as possible); Aramaic cannot show ḥ/ḫ. (3) Doctrine “statute-for-ever” states Hebrews’ and Ezekiel’s evidence side by side without resolving how עוֹלָם is meant; check the reviewer wants that framing. Leads not followed: Syriac ܚܘܩܐ “line, rule” (Wiktionary only; Payne Smith not checked, and the Peshitta New Testament has no word of this root in SEDRA); Ge’ez ḥaqaqa “fasten” (Anderson–Moser SEM000754) and ሕግ ḥəgg “law” (Wiktionary) not checked in Dillmann or Leslau; no Akkadian, Ugaritic or Phoenician cognate found. James 4:12 νομοθέτης is not the Septuagint’s rendering of Isa 33:22 (ἄρχων), so it is used in doctrine only, not as a Greek rendering. The poel “ruler’s staff” sense of מְחֹקֵק has no cognate or kin, so lexicon-support counts the root’s cognates against it; its tie to the root is through the commander who holds it (Num 21:18 sets it beside מִשְׁעֲנֹת, staffs).
